title: Children of Men
synopsis: Eighteen years of infertility, a London under refugee crackdown, and a woman in a barn who is the first impossible mother.

nodes.text: The screens have run the same footage since six: a boy of eighteen, the youngest person alive, stabbed outside a bar in Buenos Aires over an autograph. The newsreaders have given up pretending to know what to say. You queue, get your coffee, tip a measure of something into it on the pavement, and take four steps. Then the shopfront comes out into the street and the noise takes your hearing with it.

choices.consequence: You walk away from it with your ears ringing and a coffee still in your hand, because you have somewhere to be and this is Tuesday.
You go back toward the smoke with everyone else running the other way, and there is nothing you know how to do when you get there.

nodes.text: Jasper's house is at the end of a track behind camouflage netting: newspaper cuttings floor to ceiling, a grow lamp in the back room, a dog with bad hips. Janice sits in the chair by the window where he put her, gone since her interrogation, blinking at the trees. He brushes her hair and tells her the same jokes. In the drawer there is a government suicide kit, for later, for both of them.

choices.consequence: You stay, get comprehensively stoned, and sleep on a sofa under a coat for the first unbroken eight hours in about a year.
You leave before it gets light because staying means talking about your son, and Jasper is the only person left who would.

nodes.text: A van takes you off the street with a bag over your head, and it turns out to belong to your ex-wife. Julian across a table in a dark room: older, calmer, running the Fishes now, with men behind her who defer to her. She wants transit papers for one refugee girl. She names a figure. Neither of you mentions the funeral, so she asks after your cousin instead.

choices.consequence: You say yes for money and then discover, somewhere around the second sentence, that the money was never the reason you said it.
You tell her to find somebody else, and she lets you get almost to the door before saying your son's name.

nodes.text: Your cousin runs the Ministry of Art out of a converted power station full of whatever got rescued: a statue missing an arm, a nine-metre canvas of a bombed town hung where the turbines were. Dinner is excellent. His son sits at the table on a heavy pill regimen and says nothing at all. You ask for a joint permit, lie about a girlfriend, and he signs while explaining that he simply does not think about it.

choices.consequence: You take the papers and eat the rest of the meal with a man who saves paintings for a world that has stopped producing people.
You push him on what any of it is for once nobody is left to look at it, and the wine goes very quiet on both sides of the table.

nodes.text: The car is a battered saloon on a wooded road with four of you inside and a game going where somebody bounces a ball off the windscreen into a mouth. Everyone is genuinely, briefly happy. Ninety seconds of it. Then a burning car rolls out of the trees ahead and there are people coming down the verge with bricks and lengths of pipe, and reverse will not engage the first time.

choices.consequence: You keep your voice flat, get the door locked, and tell Luke the gear he needs, twice, until his hand actually finds it.
You are shouting before you know you are shouting, which does nothing useful and which you will remember for the rest of your life.

nodes.text: Two men on a motorbike come up on the left and the shot goes through her throat. A car interior is not designed for that much blood. Luke is driving. Kee is screaming. You have both hands pressed on a wound that will not close and you keep talking to her about nothing while it stops being relevant. And behind you the road stays empty. Nobody pursues. That is the first thing that is wrong.

choices.text: Pull her out of the car
choices.consequence: You drag a girl out of a car soaked to the elbows in someone else's blood, and she lets you, because you are what is available.
You sit in the wet seat while the fields go past and you do not look at anybody, and Kee watches you not looking.

nodes.text: The Fishes hole up at a farm, and Kee takes you out to the byre among the cows and lifts her dress. Eight months. Nobody on this planet has been pregnant for eighteen years. She says she does not know who the father is, quite flatly, then laughs at your face, and then she is nineteen years old and frightened and asking what happens next.

choices.consequence: You promise a teenager in a cowshed something no government on Earth could deliver, and you hear yourself do it, and you mean it.
You sit down hard on a milking stool and cry in front of a girl who was hoping for an adult, and she waits it out.

nodes.text: Luke lays out the Human Project: a hospital ship called Tomorrow standing off Bexhill, doctors, an island, a rendezvous at a buoy. Then he lays out the other plan — a black girl who gave birth in a British camp, held up in front of an uprising as a banner. He is twenty-four. He carries a rifle he clearly enjoys. He has already held a vote about Julian.

choices.consequence: You agree with everything he says, out loud, warmly, while working out where the keys to the car are kept.
You ask one question too many about who else voted, and he answers pleasantly, and after that he knows where you stand.

nodes.text: You hear it through a floorboard at two in the morning: the roadblock was theirs, the shot was theirs, the vote was carried, and they intend to keep the girl and the baby. Downstairs there is a car with no keys in it, a nineteen-year-old whose contractions have started, and a midwife named Miriam who wants out as badly as you do. The dogs in the yard know your smell.

choices.consequence: You get all three of them into a car and roll it down the slope in neutral before starting it, and nobody upstairs wakes.
You lie in the dark for another hour weighing it, and by dawn there is a man with a rifle sitting on the stairs.

nodes.text: You reach Jasper's before it is properly light, three of you, and he feeds everybody and asks nothing that matters. Kee eats two plates and half of yours. Miriam falls asleep upright at the table. He tells a long unfunny story about a strain of weed he grows for Janice, and gets an actual laugh out of a pregnant teenager, which is more than anyone has managed in a week.

choices.consequence: You take the bed for four hours and wake up with the dog on your feet, and it is the last quiet you will get.
You want to be gone by dusk, and Jasper argues, and you win, and Kee goes back to the car without finishing her tea.

nodes.text: Headlights come up the track in the grey light, with dogs and with men who do not bother shouting. Jasper walks out onto his own path to keep them standing there. Through the trees you can see him talking, using his hands, doing the routine. And then he lifts one arm in a small wave toward the treeline, where you are lying in wet leaves with your hand over Kee's mouth.

choices.consequence: You take the girl and go, downhill, through the netting, and you do not turn round when the single shot comes.
You get halfway back up the slope before Miriam has you by the collar, and the shot happens while she is holding you down.

nodes.text: Bexhill takes people in on cattle wagons and unloads them into a walled seaside town with soldiers on the roofs. Syd is a border guard who trades in favours and talks about appalling things in a cheerful, chatty way, like a man discussing football. Two hundred euros gets three people through as detainees. Miriam handles the paperwork. Kee's contractions are eight minutes apart and getting closer.

choices.consequence: You pay a man who thinks all of this is a great laugh, and you laugh along with him, because that is the price on top of the price.
You spend two hours looking for a cleaner route and find nothing, and come back to Syd, who has helpfully raised the fee.

nodes.text: At the gate Miriam makes a scene to pull the guards off Kee, and you watch her taken through a doorway with a hood already over her head. Inside: mud, half a mosque, graffiti in three alphabets, and an uprising due at any hour. On a wet street a woman called Marichka looks once at Kee's belly, says something in Romanian, and starts giving orders.

choices.consequence: You follow a stranger through a camp full of armed men because she is the only person here who has seen a birth.
You try to find somewhere with a door and a lock instead, and lose ten minutes that Kee's body was not prepared to lend you.

nodes.text: A room upstairs with a mattress, a bucket, and a window that will not shut. No doctor, no drugs, no clean water, no plan. You hold her under the arms and count while she pushes and swears at you in two languages. It comes out grey and slick and silent for four seconds that last considerably longer. Then there is a sound nobody in this building has heard for eighteen years.

choices.consequence: You stand in the doorway with your back to the room and your hand on the latch, listening, doing the only job you can do.
You get both hands under a head the size of an orange and take the whole weight of the first newborn in a generation.

nodes.text: The building is being cleared floor by floor by men with rifles up. You come down through it with a newborn wrapped inside a coat, and the crying carries a long way in a stairwell. Soldiers stop. One of them crosses himself. Two hundred people flatten against the walls to make a channel, and a nineteen-year-old girl walks down through it with everybody staring at what she is holding.

choices.consequence: You go one step at a time with a hand out in front of you, and the slowness is the only thing keeping anyone from firing.
You take the last flight too fast and somebody's rifle comes up, and the crying is the reason it goes back down.

nodes.text: Outside, the square is a firefight: a tank tracking its turret, an armoured car, men shooting out of upper windows. Then the noise falls away in a wave, outward from the sound of a baby. The turret stops moving. A line of soldiers steps back off the road to let you through. You walk down the middle of it. And then, roughly a minute later, somebody starts shooting again.

choices.consequence: You keep walking at the pace of a man crossing a car park, and a war holds its breath for as long as your nerve does.
You break into a run at the far kerb, and the spell goes with you, and the square comes back to life behind your heels.

nodes.text: A rowing boat tied at the end of a groyne, fog on the water, a compass, a plastic bottle. The rendezvous is a buoy somewhere offshore at some hour nobody could be specific about. Behind you the camp is being shelled by the government that built it. Kee sits in the stern with the baby inside her coat and asks whether you actually know how to do this.

choices.consequence: You tell her the truth, which is no, and she nods, and the two of you push off anyway on a falling tide.
You get the oars into the rowlocks and start pulling before she can ask again, because rowing is at least an answer.

nodes.text: The outboard drowns two hundred metres out, so it is oars. Your hands blister inside minutes. There is a hole in your side you have not looked at since the stairwell and it goes through you on every stroke, hot, then cold, then hot. Kee talks quietly to the baby. The fog takes the shore, then the sound of the shore, then everything except the water hitting the hull.

choices.consequence: You keep pulling long past the point where your body files a complaint, because the alternative is drifting where the shelling is.
You ship the oars for a minute that turns into six, and when you look at your palm it is dark and shining.

nodes.text: A brass needle in a tin box, swinging in the wet, and east does not obviously look like anything. There is a shape of noise out in the fog that could be an engine, or surf on shingle, or a fault in your own ears. You are pulling harder on one arm than the other without meaning to. Kee says a name for the baby out loud, twice, testing it.

choices.consequence: You steer by a needle you cannot fully see and correct every twenty strokes, which is either navigation or superstition.
You put the tin down and row toward the noise instead, on nothing but a feeling, with a girl and an infant in the boat.

nodes.text: You have long stopped counting strokes. Then the fog thins in one place and a hull comes out of it — grey, enormous, streaked with rust, a name riveted to the bow that you can nearly read. Kee is standing up in a rowing boat, which is a terrible idea, and shouting. Your right hand has stopped closing properly on the oar. Your breath will not go past whatever is in your side.

choices.consequence: You get one arm up and wave at a ship the size of a street, and somewhere above you a light swings round onto the boat.
You put a hand on Kee's leg to make her sit down, because after all this, capsizing forty metres from the ship would be exactly right.

nodes.text: The baby is asleep against Kee's collarbone with one fist out of the blanket, and the fog is going pale gold at the edges. Small flat nose. Absurd eyelashes. Somebody on the deck above is paying out a line. You have been awake for three days, and there is a warmth spreading under your coat that you are choosing not to investigate, and everything has gone rather quiet and quite comfortable.

choices.consequence: You keep your eyes open on purpose for one more minute, because you would like the last thing to be that face and not the water.
You lie back against the transom and let the boat rock, and Kee is still talking to you, and you have stopped answering.
You think about a man in a cottage waving at a treeline, and how he made the same decision, and how cheerful he managed to be about it.

nodes.text: The line comes down and a doctor in a fleece takes the baby up the gangway first, then Kee, who will not let go of the rail until she can see where they have put her. A sailor gets your coat open, swears at what is underneath it, and packs the wound with something cold while shouting for a stretcher. The grey sea goes on doing exactly what it did before, indifferent, and today that indifference has let three people through.

You lie back in the bottom of the boat with the water knocking against the boards, and the fog turns pink at the edges the way it does over the Channel in the early morning. Kee is holding the baby up so you can see, and saying the name again, and the small face is doing something that is probably wind. For one breath the world is a thing that has been started over. You do not need the next breath particularly.

You surface in the back bedroom of a cottage with the smell of frying and Jasper in the doorway with a teapot, complaining that you slept through the good part of the news. Janice is at the window in the sun. The dog is on your feet. Somewhere outside, an entire war has quietly finished being necessary, and the baby in your arms grins at the ceiling for no reason at all, the way they apparently do.
